title: Integrals Resulting in Inverse Trigonometric Functions
lead: The derivatives of the inverse trigonometric functions turn into three integration formulas, for integrands built from a² − u², a² + u² and u² − a². With substitution to bring an integrand into one of these forms, they give antiderivatives that are inverse sines, tangents and secants.
objectives: Integrate functions resulting in inverse trigonometric functions
summary_html:
• Formulas for derivatives of inverse trigonometric functions developed in Derivatives of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions lead directly to integration formulas involving inverse trigonometric functions.
  • Use the formulas listed in the rule on integration formulas resulting in inverse trigonometric functions to match up the correct format and make alterations as necessary to solve the problem.
  • Substitution is often required to put the integrand in the correct form.

Explain the relationship $-\cos^{-1}t+C=\int \frac{dt}{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}}=\sin^{-1}t+C.$ Is it true, in general, that $\cos^{-1}t=-\sin^{-1}t?$

answer.solution: $\cos(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta )=\sin\theta .$ So, $\sin^{-1}t=\frac{\pi}{2}-\cos^{-1}t.$ They differ by a constant.

exercises.prompt: Explain the relationship $\sec^{-1}t+C=\int \frac{dt}{|t|\sqrt{t^{2}-1}}=-\csc^{-1}t+C.$ Is it true, in general, that $\sec^{-1}t=-\csc^{-1}t?$

answer.solution: Since $\csc(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta)=\sec\theta,$ $\sec^{-1}t=\frac{\pi}{2}-\csc^{-1}t$ for $|t|\ge 1:$ $\sec^{-1}t$ and $-\csc^{-1}t$ are two antiderivatives of $\frac{1}{|t|\sqrt{t^{2}-1}}$ that differ by the constant $\frac{\pi}{2},$ which the constants of integration absorb. So it is not true in general that $\sec^{-1}t=-\csc^{-1}t;$ the two differ by $\frac{\pi}{2}.$

exercises.prompt: Explain what is wrong with the following integral: $\int_{1}^{2}\frac{dt}{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}}.$

answer.solution: $\sqrt{1-t^{2}}$ is not defined as a real number when $t\gt 1.$

exercises.prompt: Explain what is wrong with the following integral: $\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{dt}{|t|\sqrt{t^{2}-1}}.$

answer.solution: The integrand $\frac{1}{|t|\sqrt{t^{2}-1}}$ is not a real number for $|t|\lt 1,$ and at $t=\pm 1$ its denominator is zero, so it is defined at no point of $[-1,1]$ and the integral has no meaning, as in Exercise 405.

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, solve for the antiderivative $\int f$ of $\kf$ with $C=0,$ then use a calculator to graph $\kf$ and the antiderivative over the given interval $[a,b].$ Identify a value of C such that adding C to the antiderivative recovers the definite integral $F(x)=\int_{a}^{x}\kf(t)dt.$

[T] $\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{9-x^{2}}}dx$ over $[-3,3]$

answer.solution: The antiderivative is $\sin^{-1}(\frac{x}{3})+C.$ Taking $C=\frac{\pi}{2}$ recovers the definite integral.

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, solve for the antiderivative $\int f$ of $\kf$ with $C=0,$ then use a calculator to graph $\kf$ and the antiderivative over the given interval $[a,b].$ Identify a value of C such that adding C to the antiderivative recovers the definite integral $F(x)=\int_{a}^{x}\kf(t)dt.$

[T] $\int \frac{\cos x}{4+\sin^{2}x}dx$ over $[-6,6]$

answer.solution: The antiderivative is $\frac{1}{2}\;\tan^{-1}(\frac{\sin x}{2})+C.$ Taking $C=\frac{1}{2}\;\tan^{-1}(\frac{\sin(6)}{2})$ recovers the definite integral.

Use the substitution $u=\sqrt{2}\;\cot x$ and the identity $1+\cot^{2}x=\csc^{2}x$ to evaluate $\int \frac{dx}{1+\cos^{2}x}.$ (Hint: Multiply the top and bottom of the integrand by $\csc^{2}x.)$

answer.solution: Using the hint, one has $\int \frac{\csc^{2}x}{\csc^{2}x+\cot^{2}x}dx=\int \frac{\csc^{2}x}{1+2\cot^{2}x}dx.$ Set $u=\sqrt{2}\cot x.$ Then, $du=-\sqrt{2}\csc^{2}x$ and the integral is $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{du}{1+u^{2}}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\tan^{-1}u+C=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\;\tan^{-1}(\sqrt{2}\cot x)+C.$ If one uses the identity $\tan^{-1}s+\tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{s})=\frac{\pi}{2},$ then this can also be written $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\;\tan^{-1}(\frac{\tan x}{\sqrt{2}})+C.$

exercises.prompt: [T] Approximate the points at which the graphs of $\kf(x)=x^{2}-1$ and ${\kg(x)=(x^{2}+1)}^{\frac{1}{2}}$ intersect to four decimal places, and approximate the area between their graphs to three decimal places.

answer.solution: $x\approx \pm1.7321.$ The left endpoint estimate with $N=100$ is 4.781 and these decimals persist for $N=500.$

exercises.prompt: Use the following graph to prove that $\int_{0}^{x}\sqrt{1-t^{2}}dt=\frac{1}{2}x\sqrt{1-x^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\;\sin^{-1}x.$

answer.solution: For $0\le x\le 1,$ the region under $y=\sqrt{1-t^{2}}$ from $0$ to $x$ is the triangle with vertices $(0,0),$ $(x,0)$ and $(x,\sqrt{1-x^{2}})$ together with the sector of the unit disk between the $y$-axis and the radius to $(x,\sqrt{1-x^{2}}).$ The triangle has area $\frac{1}{2}x\sqrt{1-x^{2}}.$ The sector’s angle $\theta,$ measured from the $y$-axis, has $\sin\theta=x,$ so $\theta=\sin^{-1}x,$ and a sector of the unit circle has area $\frac{1}{2}\theta.$ Adding, $\int_{0}^{x}\sqrt{1-t^{2}}dt=\frac{1}{2}x\sqrt{1-x^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\sin^{-1}x.$
